They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. It is in the file `/app/datapaper.pdf`\n  - A recent paper that uses this dataset is \"Brain-wide analysis reveals movement encoding structured across and within brain areas\". It is in the file `/app/methodpaper.pdf`\n  - A white paper about spike sorting and quality control is in the file `/app/ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n- **Code**:\n  - `/app/code` contains code from `/app/methodpaper.pdf`.\n- **Data** from the papers are in the directory `/app/data`.\n- **Documentation** on the **NWB** file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io. Documentation about `pynwb` is at https://pynwb.readthedocs.io/en/stable/. `pynwb` documentation is also downloaded to `/app/pynwb_docs/`.\n\n## Decoder Task\n\n- Temporally align based on **Go cue onset**. \n- Extract **2.5 s before to 1.5 s after** the go cue for each trial\n- Use **50-ms-width bins** for computing firing rates. \n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n- Time from **tone onset** in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n- Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n- Lick direction **choice** (left, right, no lick, per-trial)\n- **Outcome** (ignore, miss, hit, per-trial)\n- **Early lick** (no, yes, per-trial)\n- **Tongue y-position**, per-session discretization:\n  - 0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 1: 40th to 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 2: > 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 3: not visible\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. It is in the file `/app/datapaper.pdf`\n  - A recent paper that uses this dataset is \"Brain-wide analysis reveals movement encoding structured across and within brain areas\". It is in the file `/app/methodpaper.pdf`\n  - A white paper about spike sorting and quality control is in the file `/app/ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \n- **Code**:\n  - `/app/code` contains code from `/app/methodpaper.pdf`.\n- **Data** from the papers are in the directory `/app/data`.\n- **Documentation** on the **NWB** file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io. Documentation about `pynwb` is at https://pynwb.readthedocs.io/en/stable/. `pynwb` documentation is also downloaded to `/app/pynwb_docs/`.\n\n## Decoder Task\n\n- Temporally align based on **Go cue onset**. \n- Extract **2.5 s before to 1.5 s after** the go cue for each trial\n- Use **50-ms-width bins** for computing firing rates. \n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n- Time from **tone onset** in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n- Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n- Lick direction **choice** (left, right, no lick, per-trial)\n- **Outcome** (ignore, miss, hit, per-trial)\n- **Early lick** (no, yes, per-trial)\n- **Tongue y-position**, per-session discretization:\n  - 0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 1: 40th to 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 2: > 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n  - 3: not visible\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n\n### Consistency requirements\n\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n- Loading of data\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\n\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference papers and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n\n---\n\n## Conversion Workflow\n\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. For each good unit, the bin edges for every trial are built as one flat array of absolute times, `np.searchsorted` gives the running spike count at each edge, and differencing adjacent counts gives the spike count per bin. Counts are divided by the bin width to give Hz. No smoothing, normalisation, or baseline subtraction is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    # running spike total at each edge; differencing gives the count per bin\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\nrates /= BIN                                  # counts -> Hz\n```\n\niii. Firing rate is computed from the binned spike count over the 50 ms window defined in the instructions. This also matches the reference code, which calls `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` and returns `binSpikes / bin_width`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Only units with `units/classification == 'good'` are kept. No thresholds are applied to any individual quality metric. A session with no such units is dropped entirely. This retains 69,453 of 272,227 units (25.5%), a median of 390 per session.\n\nii.\n```python\n# ---- units: QC classifier verdict ----------------------------------\ncls = _text(units['classification'])\ngood = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\nif good.size == 0:\n    return None\n```\n\niii. `classification` is the verdict of the spike-sorting quality-control classifier described in `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`.\n\n`units/unit_quality` ('good' / 'multi') is deliberately not used: it is an older label that disagrees on 12.2% of the classifier-good units and is far more permissive.\n\nThe one dropped session (`sub-440958_ses-20190216T162508`) has `classification` and `anno_name` set to NaN for all 1,852 units, i.e. it was never quality-controlled. Excluding it gives 173 sessions and 69,453 good units, against the white paper's 173 sessions and 69,943 units.\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Spike times and event times are already on the same session-absolute clock, so no alignment step is needed. The bin edges relative to the go cue are added to each trial's go-cue time to give the absolute time window for that trial, and the spikes are binned against those edges directly.\n\nii.\n```python\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n```\n\niii. There is no resampling or interpolation, and no per-stream offset to correct.\n\n## 2-e. How is the `neural` data temporally binned/resampled?\n\ni. Spike times are binned into 80 non-overlapping 50 ms bins spanning -2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue. The bin grid is defined once, as 81 edges relative to the go cue, and reused for every trial and session, so every trial has the same 80 timepoints.\n\nii.\n```python\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. The window and the 50 ms bin width are set by the instructions. Defining the grid once as offsets from the go cue gives a constant 80 timepoints per trial, which the target format requires.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* derived from?\n\ni. From `sample_start_times`, the tone onsets of the session, together with the go cue of each trial. The tone taken for a trial is the **last one** before its go cue.\n\nii.   hit = out_k == 'hit'\n310\t        miss = out_k == 'miss'\n311\t        choice[hit & (instr_k == 'left')] = CHOICE_LEFT\n312\t        choice[hit & (instr_k == 'right')] = CHOICE_RIGHT\n313\t        choice[miss & (instr_k == 'left')] = CHOICE_RIGHT\n314\t        choice[miss & (instr_k == 'right')] = CHOICE_LEFT\n315\t\n316\t        outcome_code = np.array([OUTCOME_CODE[o] for o in out_k], first assigned to the trial they were acquired in (the camera only\n369\t    runs during a trial), so a window that extends outside its own trial cannot pick up\n370\t    frames belonging to a neighbouring trial.\n371\t\n372\t    Args:\n373\t        nwb: open NWBFile.\n374\t        trial_start: (n_trials_raw,) absolute trial start times.\n375\t        go: (n_trials,) absolute go-cue times of the retained trials.\n376\t        keep_idx: (n_trials,) indices of the retained trials in the raw trials table.\n377\t\n378\t    Returns:\n379\t        (n_trials, NBINS) float array with the mean visible tongue y per bin (NaN when\n380\t        the tongue was never visible in that bin), and the fraction of visible frames.\n381\t    \"\"\"\n382\t    n_trials = len(keep_idx)\n383\t    out = np.full((n_trials, NBINS), np.nan, dtype=np.float64)\n384\t\n385\t    bts = nwb.acquisition.get('BehavioralTimeSeries', None)\n386\t    if bts is None or 'Camera0_side_TongueTracking' not in data = np.asarray(ts_obj.data[:, 1:3], dtype=np.float64)     # y, likelihood\n392\t    y = data[:, 0]\n393\t    visible = data[:, 1] > TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESH\n394\t    visible_frac = float(visible.mean()) if len(visible) else 0.0\n395\t\n396\t    # frame -> trial (video only runs within a trial; frames start at trial_start)\n397\t    frame_trial = np.searchsorted(trial_start, frame_t, side='right') - 1\n398\t\n399\t    # only visible frames matter for the value; keep them and their trial/bin index\n400\t    vis = np.flatnonzero(visible & (frame_trial >= 0))\n401\t    if len(vis) == 0:\n402\t        return out, visible_frac\n403\t    ft = frame_trial[vis]\n404\t\n405\t    # map raw trial index -> position in keep_idx (-1 when the trial was dropped)\n406\t    n_raw = len(trial_start)\n407\t    pos_of_trial = np.full(n_raw, -1, dtype=np.int64)\n408\t    pos_of_trial[keep_idx] = np.arange(n_trials)\n409\t    pos = pos_of_trial[ft]\n410\t    sel = pos >= 0\n411\t    vis, pos = vis[sel], pos[sel]\n412\t    if len(vis) == 0:\n413\t        return out, visible_frac\n414\t\n415\t    rel = frame_t[vis] - go[pos]\n416\t    inwin = (rel >= OFF_START) & (rel < OFF_END)\n417\t    vis, pos, rel = vis[inwin], pos[inwin], rel[inwin]\n418\t    if len(vis) == 0:\n419\t        return out, visible_frac\n420\t\n421\t    bin_idx = np.floor((rel - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE).astype(np.int64)\n422\t    np.clip(bin_idx, 0, NBINS - 1, out=bin_idx)\n423\t    flat = pos * NBINS + bin_idx\n424\t    n_cells = n_trials * NBINS\n425\t    sums = np.bincount(flat, weights=y[vis], minlength=n_cells)\n426\t    cnts = np.bincount(flat, minlength=n_cells)\n427\t    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):\n428\t        mean = np.where(cnts > 0, sums / np.maximum(cnts, 1), np.nan)\n429\t    out = mean.reshape(n_trials, NBINS)\n430\t    return out, visible_frac\n431\t\n432\t\n433\tdef discretise_tongue(tongue_y):\n434\t    \"\"\"Discretise tongue y into 0/1/2 by session percentiles, 3 where not visible.\"\"\"\n435\t    cls = np.full(tongue_y.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)\n436\t    vis = ~np.isnan(tongue_y)\n437\t    if vis.sum() == 0:\n438\t        return cls, (np.nan, np.nan)\n439\t    vals = tongue_y[vis]\n440\t    p_lo = np.percentile(vals, TONGUE_LOW_PCT)\n441\t    p_hi = np.percentile(vals, TONGUE_HIGH_PCT)\n442\t    v = float(p_hi))\n448\t\n449\t\n450\t# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n451\t# Plotting (--show-processing)\n452\t# ALM is defined as units on\n    ALM-targeted insertions annotated to secondary motor / primary motor / frontal-pole areas.\n    Hemisphere is stored separately in metadata rather than doubling the region list.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] 173 sessions, 28 subjects, 655 insertions, ≈ 69.4 k good units.\n- [ ] Trials/session (excluding early licks) ≈ 476.\n- [ ] Photostim trials ≈ 20 % of trials; photostim always ends before the go cue and lies in the\n      delay epoch.\n- [ ] Median tone→go interval = 1.85 s.\n- [ ] `choice` derived from (instruction, outcome) agrees with the direction of the **first lick**\n      after the go cue on ≥ 99 % of hit/miss trials, and `ignore` trials have no licks.\n- [ ] Tongue visible ≈ 6–11 % of frames; visible bins concentrated after the go cue.\n- [ ] Tongue class fractions ≈ 40 / 20 / 40 of the *visible* bins.\n- [ ] Per-neuron mean firing rate in the converted data matches `units.avg_firing_rate` in order\n      of magnitude, and a direct spike-count recomputation from the raw NWB matches exactly.\n- [ ] Neural, input and output spot-checks against the raw NWB with `np.allclose`.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py` (+ `/app/ccf_regions.py` for the CCF annotation → coarse-area map).\n\nStructure:\n- `list_session_files()` — enumerate the 174 NWB files.\n- `process_session(path)` — everything for one session; returns `None` if the session is dropped.\n- `bin_spikes_rate(spike_times, go_times)` — vectorised binning. The per-trial bin edges are\n  built as `go[:,None] + BIN_EDGES[None,:]` and located in the (sorted) spike train with a single\n  `np.searchsorted`, so there is no Python loop over trials; the counts are `np.diff` of the\n  resulting indices, divided by the bin width to give Hz.\n- `interval_overlap_bins()` — photostimulation indicator.\n- `bin_tongue()` — assigns every video frame to its trial, keeps visible frames\n  (likelihood > 0.9) inside the window, and averages `y` per (trial, bin) with two\n  `np.bincount` calls.\n- `discretise_tongue()` — 40th/60th session percentiles over the visible bins.\n- `plot_processing()` — the `--show-processing` figure (8 panels, one per processing step).\n- `main()` — `multiprocessing.Pool` over sessions (default 16 workers), assembles the final dict.\n\nBugs found and fixed while developing:\n1. **`is_good_trials` / `obs_intervals` are not always `n_trials` long.** In 9 sessions the ephys\n   recording covers only a subset of the behavioural trials (e.g. `SC015_20190208_133600_s2`:\n   160 of 480 trials). `units.obs_intervals` is identical for every unit of a session and its\n   rows match the `[start_time, stop_time]` of the *observed* trials exactly (checked for all\n   174 files). The script now locates the observed trials in the trials table by `start_time`\n   and restricts everything to them. Note 8 of the 9 are a prefix of the trials table but\n   `SC026_20190807_134913_s20` is not, so a simple \"first N trials\" rule would have been wrong.\n2. **Trials with literally no spikes.** The recording can stop part-way through the last\n   annotated trial, leaving a trial in which not one of hundreds of good units fires. Such\n   trials are dropped (1 trial in the 2-session sample; they also triggered an\n   \"all neural data is zero\" warning from the verifier).\n\nCode inefficiencies identified / speedups added:\n- Reading spike times per unit through `units['spike_times'][i]` is slow; the whole flattened\n  ragged dataset is read once (`sv.target.data[:]`, ~90 MB per session, 0.13 s) and sliced.\n- Per-trial Python loops for binning replaced by a single vectorised `np.searchsorted`.\n- Tongue binning done with `np.bincount` instead of a per-bin loop.\n- Sessions processed in parallel with `multiprocessing` (16 workers).\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nCommand: `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing`\n(2 sessions, both from subject 440956).\n\n### Sample Statistics\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Sessions | 2 |\n| Neurons (total) | 834 |\n| Neurons / session | mean 417.0 (375, 459) |\n| Subjects | 1 |\n| Trials (total) | 513 |\n| Trials / session | mean 256.5 (159, 354) |\n| T (time bins) | 80 for every trial |\n| `time_from_tone_onset` range | [-0.6, 5.7] s |\n| `photostim_on` range | [0, 1] |\n| `choice` distribution | left 0.456, right 0.407, no lick 0.136 |\n| `outcome` distribution | ignore 0.136, miss 0.298, hit 0.565 |\n| `early_lick` distribution | no 0.942, yes 0.058 |\n| `tongue_y_position` distribution | low 0.094, mid 0.047, high 0.094, not visible 0.766 |\n\nTongue classes 0/1/2 are in a 0.094 : 0.047 : 0.094 ratio = **40 : 20 : 40 of the visible bins**,\nexactly as the percentile definition requires. ✔\n\n### Processing Plots Review\n`processing_SC015_20190207_120657_s1.png`, `processing_SC015_20190208_133600_s2.png`:\n- **Alignment**: trial start is at −3.2 s (median) and the tone onset sits at exactly −1.85 s\n  (= 0.65 s sample + 1.2 s delay) on nearly every trial. ✔\n- **Firing rates**: a clear population response locked to the go cue, plus a smaller bump at\n  the sample onset (−1.85 s). Ours is a *single shared* linear readout on 100 PCs for all 173 sessions at all 80 time bins; theirs is one decoder per session **per time point**, on hand-picked pseudo-populations, with hyper-parameter selection by nested CV, and on 200 ms causally-smoothed rates instead of 50 ms bins. |\n| Choice, **delay epoch**, neural | rises through sample and delay, well above chance by the end of the delay (Fig. 6D) | [−1.2, 0] s | 0.696 (left vs right) | Same qualitative time course |\n| Choice, **sample epoch**, neural | starts at chance, rises during the sample | [−1.85, −1.2] s | 0.650 | ✔ |\n| Choice, **pre-sample**, neural | chance | [−2.5, −1.85] s | 0.540 | ✔ near chance, as it must be |\n| Choice from **video**, response epoch | AUC 0.99 ± 0.01 | response | — (video is an output here, not an input) | For reference only; AUC 0.99 ≈ 0.95 accuracy |\n| Choice from **video markers**, response epoch | 0.88 ± 0.01 | response | — | Our tongue-position output is the same marker stream |\n| Outcome, early lick, tongue position | not decoded in either paper | — | 0.659 / 0.748 / 0.662 | No published target |\n\nThe full time course reproduces the published profile of choice coding: at chance before the\ninstruction, rising through the sample and delay epochs, and jumping to its maximum ~0.3 s after\nthe go cue. The residual gap to \"close to perfect\" is fully accounted for by the decoder\narchitecture the task prescribes (one shared low-rank linear readout, no per-time-point or\nper-session fitting, no temporal smoothing); it is not a property of the converted data.\n\n### Check 3 — train vs. validation gap\n| Output | Train | Validation | Train / Val |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| choice | 0.7081 | 0.6794 | 1.042 |\n| outcome | 0.7027 | 0.6590 | 1.066 |\n| early_lick | 0.7898 | 0.7484 | 1.055 |\n| tongue_y_position | 0.6930 | 0.6619 | 1.047 |\n\nMaximum ratio 1.07, far below the 1.5 threshold: no overfitting and no sign of leakage between\nthe training and validation trials.\n\n### Per-class recall (response epoch, validation)\n| Output | Class recalls |\n|---|---|\n| choice | left 0.765, right 0.745, no lick 0.797 |\n| outcome | ignore 0.750, miss 0.780, hit 0.826 |\n| early_lick | no 0.594, yes 0.779 |\n| tongue_y_position | low 0.585, mid 0.475, high 0.700, not visible 0.617 |\n\nNo class collapses, so the balanced-loss training is working and every class is represented.\nThe `mid (40–60th pct)` tongue class is hardest, which is expected: it is the narrowest slice of\na continuous variable and is bounded on both sides by the other two classes.\n\n### Issues found and resolved in this step\nNone new. The two items examined (early_lick ratio, choice below the papers' \"near perfect\")\nwere traced to the task structure and to the prescribed decoder architecture, respectively, and\nverified not to be conversion errors. The one genuine bug found during the review phase (the\nsub-millisecond photostim/bin-edge overlap) was fixed in Step 10 and the full conversion,\nverification, sanity checks and decoder training were all re-run afterwards.\n\n### Known caveat (documented, not a bug)\nSpikes exist only inside each trial's recorded interval (`units.obs_intervals` ==\ntrials `[start_time, stop_time]`). On error (`miss`) trials the interval ends at the error lick,\nso only ~8 % of them extend to go + 1.5 s; overall 17.5 % of trials have no spikes in the last\n5 bins and 1.8 % none in the first 5. The fixed window is binned regardless — exactly what the\nreference `process_one_area` does — so those bins read 0 Hz. This inevitably makes `outcome`\npartly decodable from the position of the zero-padding rather than from neural activity alone.\nThe alternative (dropping trials without full coverage) would remove ~92 % of `miss` trials and\nleave the `outcome` output with effectively two classes, so it was rejected. The caveat is\nrecorded in `data['metadata']['caveat']`.\n\n---\n\n## Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n- [x] `README.md` created — dataset description, how to load and use the pickle, full output\n      format specification, curation summary, key statistics and decoder performance.\n- [x] `cache/` folder created with `cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting every cached file.\n- [x] All files organised.\n\n### Deliverables\n| File | Status |\n|---|---|\n| `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` | this file |\n| `/app/convert_data.py` (+ `/app/ccf_regions.py`) | conversion script |\n| `/app/converted_data.pkl` | 11.8 GB, 173 sessions |\n| `/app/sample_data.pkl` | 73 MB, 2 sessions |\n| `/app/README.md` | user-facing documentation |\n| `/app/conversion_sample_out.txt`, `/app/conversion_full_out.txt` | conversion logs |\n| `/app/verification_sample_out.txt`, `/app/verification_full_out.txt` | `--verify-only` logs (valid, no errors or warnings) |\n| `/app/train_decoder_sample_out.txt`, `/app/train_decoder_full_out.txt` | decoder training logs |\n| `/app/sanity_checks.py`, `/app/sanity_checks_out.txt` | 101 independent checks, 0 failed |\n| `/app/analyze_accuracy_vs_time.py` | per-time-bin accuracy analysis used in Step 12 |\n| `/app/processing_SC015_*.png` | per-step verification plots |\n| `/app/sample_trials.png`, `/app/predictions.png` | decoder sample/prediction plots |\n| `/app/cache/` | exploration scripts and intermediate results |\n\n### Summary of the decisions that define this conversion\n1. Step 4 and Step 10 Check 3: the reference `get_regular_trial_mask` is\n`early_lick == 0 & auto_water == 0 & free_water == 0 & correctness != -1 & stimulation == 0`.\nThe AI reasoned that three of those five clauses directly conflict with the decoder\nspecification — removing early-lick trials would leave the `early_lick` output with one class,\nremoving `correctness == -1` would delete the `ignore` class of `outcome` and the `no lick`\nclass of `choice`, and removing stimulated trials would make the `photostim` input identically\nzero — so those three are dropped and the conflict documented, while `auto_water` and\n`free_water` are applied exactly as in the reference. `obs_intervals` is the file's own record\nof which trials were recorded, so trials outside it carry no neural data at all and would\nappear as 4 s of 0 Hz. `is_good_trials` is described in Step 3 as \"the residue of [the] manual\n[drift] annotation\" at the penetration level from the QC white paper. The all-zero-spike drop\nwas found because it triggered an \"all neural data is zero\" warning from `train_decoder.py`.\nThe 2-trial minimum is the target format's stated requirement. The AI explicitly declined to\nre-apply the papers' 65% behavioural-performance session criterion, on the grounds that the\nsession and insertion counts already match the paper exactly, so the released set *is* the\nanalysed set.\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. `units/spike_times` — the sorted, session-absolute spike times of each unit, stored as a\nragged NWB `VectorData`/`VectorIndex` pair. The AI reads the flat buffer\n(`units['spike_times'].target.data`) once per session and the per-unit end offsets\n(`units['spike_times'].data`), then slices per unit. Only units with\n`classification == 'good'` contribute. The second input is\n`BehavioralEvents['go_start_times'].timestamps`, which places the bin edges.\n\nii.\n```python\n        sv = units['spike_times']\n        ends = np.asarray(sv.data[:])\n        starts = np.concatenate([[0], ends[:-1]])\n        flat_spikes = np.asarray(sv.target.data[:], dtype=np.float64)\n\n        n_neurons = len(good)\n        fr = np.empty((n_neurons, n_trials, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n        for i, u in enumerate(good):\n            st = flat_spikes[starts[u]:ends[u]]\n            fr[i] = bin_spikes_rate(st, go)\n```\n\n```python\ndef _events(nwb, name):\n    \"\"\"Timestamps of a `BehavioralEvents` TimeSeries, as a numpy array.\"\"\"\n    ts = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents'].time_series[name]\n    return np.asarray(ts.timestamps[:], dtype=np.float64)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 variable mapping: `units.spike_times` (absolute) + `go_start_times.timestamps` →\n`neural`, with the reference analogue being `process_one_area` + `sliding_histogram(rate=True)`.\nSpike times are the only neural representation in the file. Step 6 records that reading\nper-unit through `units['spike_times'][i]` is slow, so the whole flattened ragged dataset is\nread once (~90 MB/session, 0.13 s) and sliced — a ~5× speed-up on the neural step.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Spike times are converted into per-bin **firing rates in Hz**. For each good unit the\nper-trial bin edges are formed as `go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]`, flattened, and located in\nthe unit's sorted spike train with a single `np.searchsorted(..., side='left')`; differencing\nadjacent indices along the bin axis gives the spike count per bin, and dividing by 0.05 s gives\nHz. Bin *k* covers the half-open interval `[go + BIN_EDGES[k], go + BIN_EDGES[k+1])`. The\nresult is stored as `float32`. There is no smoothing, no normalisation, no baseline\nsubtraction, and no overlapping/sliding window. Bins that fall outside the recorded interval\nare binned anyway and therefore read 0 Hz.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_spikes_rate(spike_times, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Spike counts of one unit in the fixed window around every go cue, as a rate.\n    ...\n        Bin k covers [go + BIN_EDGES[k], go + BIN_EDGES[k+1]).\n    \"\"\"\n    edges = go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]           # (n_trials, NBINS+1)\n    idx = np.searchsorted(spike_times, edges.ravel(), side='left')\n    idx = idx.reshape(edges.shape)\n    counts = np.diff(idx, axis=1)\n    return (counts / BIN_SIZE).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 3 and Step 10 Check 3(d): rates in Hz (counts / 0.05 s) reproduce the\nreference `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)`, which returns `binSpikes / bin_width`. The AI\ndocuments that the counting rule, the rate normalisation and the treatment of the trial edges\n(bin the whole fixed window regardless of when the trial ended, as `process_one_area` does) are\nidentical to the reference; only the bin width and stride differ, because the task\nspecification prescribes 50 ms non-overlapping bins instead of the reference's 40 ms/3.4 ms\nsliding window. Sanity check 2 re-counted the rates bin-by-bin from the raw NWB with a\nbrute-force `np.sum((st >= lo) & (st < hi)) / 0.05` and passed with `np.allclose` on 5 sessions\n× 20 trial×neuron probes; check 3 confirmed the per-neuron mean rates correlate at r = 0.988–\n0.998 with the independent `units.avg_firing_rate` column.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Only units with `units/classification == 'good'` are kept. No threshold is applied to any\nindividual quality metric, and in particular the method paper's \"mean firing rate ≥ 2 Hz\"\ncriterion is deliberately **not** applied. A session with zero good units is dropped entirely.\nThis retains 69,453 of the ~272 k units (mean 401.5 per session, range 90–923) across 173\nsessions and 655 insertions.\n\nii.\n```python\n        units = nwb.units\n        classification = np.asarray(units['classification'][:])\n        good = np.flatnonzero(classification == 'good')\n        if len(good) == 0:\n            io.close()\n            return None\n```\n\n```python\n            'neuron_curation': (\n                \"units.classification == 'good' (region-specific logistic-regression QC \"\n                'classifiers of Chen, Liu et al. 2023 white paper); no firing-rate threshold'),\n```\n\niii. Step 3/Step 5 decision 4: `classification` is the output of the region-specific\nlogistic-regression QC classifiers described in `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`, and is\nthe same criterion as the reference code's `qc_mode='classifier'` unit index. The AI rejected\nthe method paper's ≥ 2 Hz cut because \"it was introduced to stabilise per-neuron R² estimates\nin the video→firing-rate regression, not for decoding, and discarding low-rate neurons would\nthrow away decodable information\" — and the method paper itself states the result is\ninsensitive to that threshold. Consistency evidence in Step 4/Step 9: dropping the one session\nwith zero good units (`SC017_20190216_162508_s4`, whose `classification` column is NaN\nthroughout) yields exactly the paper's 173 sessions **and** exactly 655 insertions; the unit\ntotal of 69,453 is 99.3% of the published 69,943, attributed to the DANDI release version\npost-dating the paper snapshot.\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Alignment is to **go-cue onset**, `BehavioralEvents['go_start_times'].timestamps`, one per\ntrial. Spike times and event timestamps are already on the same session-absolute clock, so no\nresampling, interpolation or per-stream offset correction is needed: the fixed grid of bin\nedges relative to the go cue is simply added to each retained trial's go-cue time, and the\nspikes are binned against those absolute edges. The same go-cue-relative grid is reused for the\ntwo inputs and for the tongue output, so bin *k* covers the same interval in every stream.\n\nii.\n```python\n        go_times = _events(nwb, 'go_start_times')\n        ...\n        go = go_times[keep_idx]\n```\n\n```python\n    edges = go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]           # (n_trials, NBINS+1)\n    idx = np.searchsorted(spike_times, edges.ravel(), side='left')\n```\n\n```python\n            'temporal_alignment_event': 'onset of the auditory go cue (go_start_times)',\n            'off_start': OFF_START,\n            'off_end': OFF_END,\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 1: \"Alignment = go cue … Matches both papers and all reference code.\"\nStep 10 Check 3(c) records that the reference `.mat` export already stores spike times relative\nto `task_cue_time[0]` (the go cue) and aligns markers by subtracting the same quantity\n(`align_markers.py`), so subtracting `go_start_times` from the NWB absolute times is the same\noperation. The `--show-processing` plot panel 1 was used to verify alignment visually: trial\nstart sits at a median −3.2 s and the tone onset at exactly −1.85 s (= 0.65 s sample + 1.2 s\ndelay) on nearly every trial, which is the expected task geometry.\n\n## 2-e. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 50 ms, i.e. 80 non-overlapping bins spanning −2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue. The\ngrid is defined once at module level as 81 edges (and 80 centres) relative to the go cue and\nreused for every trial, every session and every data stream, so every trial has exactly 80\ntimepoints. No rebinning/resampling of an intermediate representation is performed — spikes go\nstraight from raw times into the 50 ms bins, and the tongue video (~300 Hz) is averaged into the\nsame 50 ms bins in one step. `metadata['time_bin_size']` is 50.0 ms and the bin centres are\nstored in `metadata['bin_centers_s']`.\n\nii.\n```python\nOFF_START = -2.5          # s, signed time from the go cue to the start of the trial window\nOFF_END = 1.5             # s, signed time from the go cue to the end of the trial window\nBIN_SIZE = 0.05           # s\nNBINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE))          # 80\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)       # (81,)\nBIN_CENTERS = BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2                   # (80,)\n```\n\n```python\n            'time_bin_size': BIN_SIZE * 1000.0,       # ms\n            'n_time_bins': NBINS,\n            'bin_centers_s': BIN_CENTERS.tolist(),\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 2: the window and bin width are taken verbatim from the Decoder Task\nsection of the instructions. Step 9/Step 10 Check 3(d) records this as a *deliberate* departure\nfrom the reference's 40 ms width / 3.4 ms stride sliding window, justified because the task\nspecifies the binning; a single fixed grid is also what makes the \"same number of timepoints\nfor all trials and sessions\" format requirement hold. Step 10 Check 5, item 6 pins down the\nhalf-open bin convention and notes that the independent sanity check uses the same convention.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. `BehavioralEvents['sample_start_times'].timestamps` (the sample-epoch / instruction-tone\nonsets of the session) together with each trial's go-cue time. The tone assigned to a trial is\nthe **last** sample-epoch start at or before that trial's go cue, found with `searchsorted`.\nA trial with no preceding sample epoch raises a `RuntimeError` (never triggered).\n\nii.\n```python\n        # tone onset := last sample-epoch start before the go cue\n        sample_start = _events(nwb, 'sample_start_times')\n        tone_pos = np.searchsorted(sample_start, go, side='right') - 1\n        if np.any(tone_pos < 0):\n            raise RuntimeError(f'{session_id}: trial without a preceding sample epoch')\n        tone_time = sample_start[tone_pos]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 8 and Step 10 Check 5, item 7: an early lick *replays* the sample epoch, so\na trial can carry more than one sample-start event; the last replay is the instruction the\nanimal actually acted on, and the one whose delay epoch leads to the go cue. The AI validated\nthis with the task geometry: the median tone→go interval is 1.85 s = 0.65 s sample + 1.2 s\ndelay, exactly the published structure, and it notes that on replay trials the residual delay\ncan be as short as 0.1 s, which is why the input is not a constant offset. Sanity check 5\nre-verified the 1.85 s median independently from the raw NWB on 5 sessions.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. Because the bins are laid out around the go cue, the value of bin *k* on a trial is simply\nthe bin centre (relative to the go cue) plus the tone→go gap: `BIN_CENTERS[k] + (go − tone)`.\nIt is emitted as a **continuous** ramp of seconds (one value per bin), `float32`, not a binary\nonset indicator. Observed range over the full dataset: [−1.5, 11.9] s.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_CENTERS = BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2                   # (80,)\n```\n```python\n        # time from tone onset at each bin centre (seconds, continuous)\n        time_from_tone = BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone_time)[:, None]   # (n_trials, NBINS)\n```\n```python\n    inputs = [np.stack([time_from_tone[j], photostim_on[j]]).astype(np.float32)\n              for j in range(n_trials)]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 9: the task specification explicitly labels this input \"continuous,\ntime-varying\", which the AI read as overriding the general format note that \"if an input is a\ntime such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series\". Beyond locating the\ntone, no further processing is applied. Sanity check 4 verified `input[0]` equals\n`bin_centre + (go − last sample_start before go)` recomputed from the raw file\n(`np.allclose`, 5 sessions); the `--show-processing` panel 4 shows a linear ramp crossing zero\nat the tone onset.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is constructed *on* the neural bin grid: `BIN_CENTERS` are the centres of exactly the same\n80 bins whose edges (`BIN_EDGES`) are used to count spikes, laid on the same per-trial go-cue\ntimes (`go`, after trial curation). So alignment is structural — there is no separate\nalignment step, and bin *k* of the input necessarily covers the same interval as bin *k* of the\nfiring rates.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)       # (81,)\nBIN_CENTERS = BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2                   # (80,)\n```\n```python\n    edges = go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]            # neural\n```\n```python\n        time_from_tone = BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone_time)[:, None]   # input\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 3(c): both streams are re-referenced to `go_start_times` on the single\nsession-absolute NWB clock, as in the reference `align_markers.py`. The AI also guarded the\norder of operations — `go` is recomputed after every trial-curation step (including the\nzero-spike drop) *before* the inputs are built, so the input rows always correspond to the same\ntrials as the neural rows.\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Photostimulation* derived from?\n\ni. `BehavioralEvents['photostim_start_times'].timestamps` and\n`BehavioralEvents['photostim_stop_times'].timestamps` — the measured laser on/off times for the\nwhole session — together with each trial's go-cue time. The AI did *not* use the trials-table\n`photostim_onset` / `photostim_duration` string columns for the conversion, but did use them as\nan independent cross-check. Missing series are caught (`KeyError` → empty arrays) and a\nstart/stop count mismatch is warned about and leaves the input at 0.\n\nii.\n```python\n        photostim_on = np.zeros((n_trials, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n        try:\n            ps_start = _events(nwb, 'photostim_start_times')\n            ps_stop = _events(nwb, 'photostim_stop_times')\n        except KeyError:\n            ps_start = ps_stop = np.zeros(0)\n        if len(ps_start) and len(ps_start) == len(ps_stop):\n            for j, g in enumerate(go):\n                m = (ps_stop > g + OFF_START) & (ps_start < g + OFF_END)\n                if m.any():\n                    photostim_on[j] = interval_overlap_bins(ps_start[m], ps_stop[m], g)\n        elif len(ps_start) != len(ps_stop):\n            print(f'  WARNING {session_id}: photostim start/stop counts differ '\n                  f'({len(ps_start)}/{len(ps_stop)}); photostim input left at 0', flush=True)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping: the reference analogue is `task_stimulation` columns 2–3, i.e. the laser\non/off *times*, which is exactly what the `BehavioralEvents` photostim series contain — so the\nAI chose the event stream over the derived trials-table strings. Sanity checks 6 and 7 verify\nthat the set of photostim trials derived from the event stream equals the set derived from the\nindependent `trials.photostim_onset != 'N/A'` column (exact match on 5 sessions), so the two\nsources agree. Check 8 verifies photostimulation always ends before the go cue and check 9 that\nonset lies inside the delay epoch on ≥ 98% of stim trials. Overall 20.0% of trials are\nstimulated, against ~19.6% in the raw data and \"~25% on photostim sessions\" in the papers.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Photostimulation*?\n\ni. A binary (0/1) `float32` time series, one value per bin: bin *k* is 1 if a photostim\ninterval overlaps it by **more than 1 ms** (`OVERLAP_TOL`), else 0. Overlap is computed\nvectorised over bins as `min(stop, edge_hi) − max(start, edge_lo)`; intervals entirely outside\nthe window are skipped. Trials with no stimulation keep an all-zero row.\n\nii.\n```python\nOVERLAP_TOL = 1e-3               # s, minimum overlap for a bin to count as photostim-on\n```\n```python\ndef interval_overlap_bins(starts, stops, go_time):\n    \"\"\"Binary (NBINS,) indicator: 1 where a [start, stop] interval overlaps the bin.\"\"\"\n    on = np.zeros(NBINS, dtype=np.float32)\n    if len(starts) == 0:\n        return on\n    for a, b in zip(starts - go_time, stops - go_time):\n        if b <= BIN_EDGES[0] or a >= BIN_EDGES[-1]:\n            continue\n        # Overlap duration between [a, b] and every bin.  A plain \"does it touch the bin\"\n        # test would mark a bin that the interval overlaps by a fraction of a millisecond:\n        # photoinhibition ends at the go cue to within +-0.5 ms, which would otherwise\n        # switch the first post-go bin on for about half of the stimulated trials.\n        ov = np.minimum(b, BIN_EDGES[1:]) - np.maximum(a, BIN_EDGES[:-1])\n        on[ov > OVERLAP_TOL] = 1.0\n    return on\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 2 records this as a bug the sanity checks caught and fixed: photoinhibition\nends at the go cue to within ±0.5 ms and starts within ±0.5 ms of a bin edge, so the original\n\"does the interval touch this bin\" test switched the first *post*-go bin on for about half the\nstimulated trials and turned on one bin too early at the onset. Requiring > 1 ms of overlap\nremoves the artefact and makes the \"photostim always ends before the go cue\" check pass\nexactly. The AI also verified, and documented as not-a-bug, one trial whose laser onset is\n2.25 s pre-go because an early-lick replay pushed the go cue later while the laser fired at its\nusual time. The `--show-processing` panel 5 shows the stimulation confined to the delay epoch\n(−1.2 to −0.7 s) on 77/354 trials in the sample session.\n\n## 4-c. How is the `input` *Photostimulation* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The laser start/stop times are converted to go-cue-relative seconds (`starts - go_time`,\n`stops - go_time`) and compared against the same `BIN_EDGES` grid used to bin the spikes, for\nthe same curated `go` array. Only intervals overlapping the trial's own [−2.5, +1.5] s window\nare considered. So alignment is again structural, on one shared grid.\n\nii.\n```python\n            for j, g in enumerate(go):\n                m = (ps_stop > g + OFF_START) & (ps_start < g + OFF_END)\n                if m.any():\n                    photostim_on[j] = interval_overlap_bins(ps_start[m], ps_stop[m], g)\n```\n```python\n    for a, b in zip(starts - go_time, stops - go_time):\n        ...\n        ov = np.minimum(b, BIN_EDGES[1:]) - np.maximum(a, BIN_EDGES[:-1])\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 3(e): the reference also re-references `task_stimulation` to the go cue; the\nonly difference is that the reference keeps it as per-trial scalars while this conversion\nrasterises it onto the bin grid, \"because the decoder wants time-varying inputs\". Because the\ncomparison is against `BIN_EDGES` rather than `BIN_CENTERS`, the sub-millisecond tolerance\n(4-b) was needed to keep the rasterisation from leaking one bin past the go cue.\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction choice* derived from?\n\ni. There is no lick-direction column in the trials table, so choice is derived from two\ncolumns: `trials.trial_instruction` (`'left'`/`'right'`, the side the tone instructed) and\n`trials.outcome` (`'hit'`/`'miss'`/`'ignore'`). A hit means the animal licked the instructed\nside, a miss means it licked the other side, and an `ignore` means it did not lick.\n\nii.\n```python\n        instruction = np.asarray(trials['trial_instruction'][:])\n        outcome = np.asarray(trials['outcome'][:])\n...\n        instr_k = instruction[keep_idx]\n        out_k = outcome[keep_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 4 (discrepancy table, \"`outcome` semantics\") documents that the AI validated this\nderivation against the raw lick-time streams before adopting it: on `hit` trials the animal\nlicks the instructed port (100%), on `miss` trials it *first* licks the opposite port (100%),\nand on `ignore` trials there are no licks in [go, go+1.5] (100%). Sanity check 13 re-ran the\nfirst-post-go-lick comparison on 5 spot-check sessions and got 100% agreement (195/195,\n353/353, 578/578, 573/573, …), and check 14 confirmed zero licks on \"no lick\" trials. So the\nderived variable is equivalent to the directly measured lick direction.\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction choice*?\n\ni. Coded 0 = left, 1 = right, 2 = no lick, with the default being `no lick` and hit/miss trials\noverwritten by the four instruction × outcome combinations. The per-trial value is then\nbroadcast across all 80 bins as row 0 of the per-trial output array (`int64`), and\n`output_values[0] = ['left', 'right', 'no lick']` names the codes. Resulting distribution:\nleft 0.429, right 0.422, no lick 0.149.\n\nii.\n```python\nCHOICE_LEFT, CHOICE_RIGHT, CHOICE_NOLICK = 0, 1, 2\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ['left', 'right', 'no lick'],\n    ...\n]\n```\n```python\n        # choice: hit -> instructed side, miss -> opposite side, ignore -> no lick\n        choice = np.full(n_trials, CHOICE_NOLICK, dtype=np.int64)\n        hit = out_k == 'hit'\n        miss = out_k == 'miss'\n        choice[hit & (instr_k == 'left')] = CHOICE_LEFT\n        choice[hit & (instr_k == 'right')] = CHOICE_RIGHT\n        choice[miss & (instr_k == 'left')] = CHOICE_RIGHT\n        choice[miss & (instr_k == 'right')] = CHOICE_LEFT\n```\n```python\n    outputs = [np.stack([np.full(NBINS, choice[j]),\n                         np.full(NBINS, outcome_code[j]),\n                         np.full(NBINS, early_code[j]),\n                         tongue_class[j]]).astype(np.int64)\n               for j in range(n_trials)]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 12: per-trial outputs are broadcast across time because the output array\nmust have a single `(n_output, n_timepoints)` shape and the tongue output is genuinely\ntime-varying. The left/right/no-lick coding follows the instructions' ordering. The AI notes in\nStep 9 that the near-equal left/right split (0.429/0.422) is the expected signature of randomly\ninterleaved trial types, which it used as a consistency check.\n\n## 6-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?\n\ni. Directly from `trials.outcome`, which already stores exactly the three strings the\ninstructions ask for: `'ignore'`, `'miss'`, `'hit'`.\n\nii.\n```python\n        outcome = np.asarray(trials['outcome'][:])\n...\n        out_k = outcome[keep_idx]\n```\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Four steps, all in `bin_tongue()`:\n1. Frames with DeepLabCut likelihood ≤ 0.9 are discarded — when the tongue is retracted the\n   tracker still reports a position, so those frames are not real measurements.\n2. Every frame is bucketed into the trial it was acquired in\n   (`searchsorted(trial_start, frame_t, 'right') - 1`), and frames belonging to trials that\n   were dropped by curation are discarded. A frame can therefore only contribute to *its own*\n   trial's window, never to a neighbour's.\n3. Surviving visible frames are mapped to `(trial, bin)` cells and the mean `y` per cell is\n   computed with two `np.bincount` calls (sums / counts).\n4. A cell with no visible frame stays NaN, which becomes the \"not visible\" class in\n   `discretise_tongue`.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESH = 0.9   # DeepLabCut likelihood above which the tongue is \"visible\"\n```\n```python\n    # frame -> trial (video only runs within a trial; frames start at trial_start)\n    frame_trial = np.searchsorted(trial_start, frame_t, side='right') - 1\n\n    # only visible frames matter for the value; keep them and their trial/bin index\n    vis = np.flatnonzero(visible & (frame_trial >= 0))\n    ...\n    pos_of_trial = np.full(n_raw, -1, dtype=np.int64)\n    pos_of_trial[keep_idx] = np.arange(n_trials)\n    pos = pos_of_trial[ft]\n    sel = pos >= 0\n    vis, pos = vis[sel], pos[sel]\n    ...\n    bin_idx = np.floor((rel - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE).astype(np.int64)\n    np.clip(bin_idx, 0, NBINS - 1, out=bin_idx)\n    flat = pos * NBINS + bin_idx\n    n_cells = n_trials * NBINS\n    sums = np.bincount(flat, weights=y[vis], minlength=n_cells)\n    cnts = np.bincount(flat, minlength=n_cells)\n    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):\n        mean = np.where(cnts > 0, sums / np.maximum(cnts, 1), np.nan)\n    out = mean.reshape(n_trials, NBINS)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 10: \"The likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (≈ 3–6 × 10⁻⁵ vs\n≈ 1.0); any threshold in [0.1, 0.99] gives the same answer to within 0.1% of frames\", so the\nexact cut is immaterial — ~6–11% of frames have the tongue visible. Step 10 Check 5, item 8\ngives the rationale for the trial bucketing: \"frames are first bucketed by trial … so a window\nthat extends past its own trial boundary cannot pick up a neighbouring trial's frames.\" Step 3\nrecords the reference's treatment (\"when the tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth …\nwe set the tongue position to its mean value\") and the AI's reading that occlusion is thereby\nan explicit distinct state, matching the required \"not visible\" class; the AI argues in Step 10\nCheck 3(f) that an explicit class \"is the more informative encoding of the same fact\" than the\nreference's mean imputation. `np.bincount` aggregation is also a Step 6 speed-up\n(~50× vs a per-bin loop).\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles are taken over *all visible binned values* of that\nsession's retained trials (i.e. the non-NaN entries of the `(n_trials, 80)` bin-mean array —\nthe same quantity that is being discretised). Each bin is then labelled 0 if its value is\nstrictly below the 40th percentile, 2 if strictly above the 60th, 1 otherwise, and 3 if it has\nno visible frame. The two percentile values are stored per session in\n`metadata['session_info'][i]['tongue_pct_40_60']`. Resulting distribution across the dataset:\n0.098 / 0.049 / 0.098 / 0.755, i.e. exactly 40 : 20 : 40 of the visible bins.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LOW_PCT = 40              # percentile boundaries for the tongue-y discretisation\nTONGUE_HIGH_PCT = 60\n```\n```python\ndef discretise_tongue(tongue_y):\n    \"\"\"Discretise tongue y into 0/1/2 by session percentiles, 3 where not visible.\"\"\"\n    cls = np.full(tongue_y.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)\n    vis = ~np.isnan(tongue_y)\n    if vis.sum() == 0:\n        return cls, (np.nan, np.nan)\n    vals = tongue_y[vis]\n    p_lo = np.percentile(vals, TONGUE_LOW_PCT)\n    p_hi = np.percentile(vals, TONGUE_HIGH_PCT)\n    v = tongue_y[vis]\n    c = np.ones(v.shape, dtype=np.int64)\n    c[v < p_lo] = 0\n    c[v > p_hi] = 2\n    cls[vis] = c\n    return cls, (float(p_lo), float(p_hi))\n```\n```python\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ...\n    ['low (<40th pct)', 'mid (40-60th pct)', 'high (>60th pct)', 'not visible'],\n]\n```\n\niii. Step 5 decision 11: \"Tongue percentiles are computed per session over the *binned, visible*\nvalues of all retained trials of that session (the quantity actually being discretised)\" — the\nper-session scope and the 40/60 split come straight from the instructions, and taking the\npercentiles of the binned rather than the raw-frame values keeps the edges on the same\nquantity that is classified. Frames where the tongue is retracted are excluded first, because\nincluding them would shift the percentiles and mix noise with real protrusions. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Spike times are converted into per-bin **firing rates in Hz**. For each good unit the\nper-trial bin edges are formed as `go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]`, flattened, and located in\nthe unit's sorted spike train with a single `np.searchsorted(..., side='left')`; differencing\nadjacent indices along the bin axis gives the spike count per bin, and dividing by 0.05 s gives\nHz. Bin *k* covers the half-open interval `[go + BIN_EDGES[k], go + BIN_EDGES[k+1])`. The\nresult is stored as `float32`. There is no smoothing, no normalisation, no baseline\nsubtraction, and no overlapping/sliding window. Bins that fall outside the recorded interval\nare binned anyway and therefore read 0 Hz.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_spikes_rate(spike_times, go_times):\n    \"\"\"Spike counts of one unit in the fixed window around every go cue, as a rate.\n    ...\n        Bin k covers [go + BIN_EDGES[k], go + BIN_EDGES[k+1]).\n    \"\"\"\n    edges = go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]           # (n_trials, NBINS+1)\n    idx = np.searchsorted(spike_times, edges.ravel(), side='left')\n    idx = idx.reshape(edges.shape)\n    counts = np.diff(idx, axis=1)\n    return (counts / BIN_SIZE).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. How is the `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is constructed *on* the neural bin grid: `BIN_CENTERS` are the centres of exactly the same\n80 bins whose edges (`BIN_EDGES`) are used to count spikes, laid on the same per-trial go-cue\ntimes (`go`, after trial curation). So alignment is structural — there is no separate\nalignment step, and bin *k* of the input necessarily covers the same interval as bin *k* of the\nfiring rates.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)       # (81,)\nBIN_CENTERS = BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2                   # (80,)\n```\n```python\n    edges = go_times[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]            # neural\n```\n```python\n        time_from_tone = BIN_CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone_time)[:, None]   # input\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 3(c): both streams are re-referenced to `go_start_times` on the single\nsession-absolute NWB clock, as in the reference `align_markers.py`. The AI also guarded the\norder of operations — `go` is recomputed after every trial-curation step (including the\nzero-spike drop) *before* the inputs are built, so the input rows always correspond to the same\ntrials as the neural rows.\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Photostimulation* derived from?\n\ni. `BehavioralEvents['photostim_start_times'].timestamps` and\n`BehavioralEvents['photostim_stop_times'].timestamps` — the measured laser on/off times for the\nwhole session — together with each trial's go-cue time. The AI did *not* use the trials-table\n`photostim_onset` / `photostim_duration` string columns for the conversion, but did use them as\nan independent cross-check. Missing series are caught (`KeyError` → empty arrays) and a\nstart/stop count mismatch is warned about and leaves the input at 0.\n\nii.\n```python\n        photostim_on = np.zeros((n_trials, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n        try:\n            ps_start = _events(nwb, 'photostim_start_times')\n            ps_stop = _events(nwb, 'photostim_stop_times')\n        except KeyError:\n            ps_start = ps_stop = np.zeros(0)\n        if len(ps_start) and len(ps_start) == len(ps_stop):\n            for j, g in enumerate(go):\n                m = (ps_stop > g + OFF_START) & (ps_start < g + OFF_END)\n                if m.any():\n                    photostim_on[j] = interval_overlap_bins(ps_start[m], ps_stop[m], g)\n        elif len(ps_start) != len(ps_stop):\n            print(f'  WARNING {session_id}: photostim start/stop counts differ '\n                  f'({len(ps_start)}/{len(ps_stop)}); photostim input left at 0', flush=True)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping: the reference analogue is `task_stimulation` columns 2–3, i.e. the laser\non/off *times*, which is exactly what the `BehavioralEvents` photostim series contain — so the\nAI chose the event stream over the derived trials-table strings. Sanity checks 6 and 7 verify\nthat the set of photostim trials derived from the event stream equals the set derived from the\nindependent `trials.photostim_onset != 'N/A'` column (exact match on 5 sessions), so the two\nsources agree. Check 8 verifies photostimulation always ends before the go cue and check 9 that\nonset lies inside the delay epoch on ≥ 98% of stim trials. Overall 20.0% of trials are\nstimulated, against ~19.6% in the raw data and \"~25% on photostim sessions\" in the papers.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Photostimulation*?\n\ni. A binary (0/1) `float32` time series, one value per bin: bin *k* is 1 if a photostim\ninterval overlaps it by **more than 1 ms** (`OVERLAP_TOL`), else 0. Overlap is computed\nvectorised over bins as `min(stop, edge_hi) − max(start, edge_lo)`; intervals entirely outside\nthe window are skipped. Trials with no stimulation keep an all-zero row.\n\nii.\n```python\nOVERLAP_TOL = 1e-3               # s, minimum overlap for a bin to count as photostim-on\n```\n```python\ndef interval_overlap_bins(starts, stops, go_time):\n    \"\"\"Binary (NBINS,) indicator: 1 where a [start, stop] interval overlaps the bin.\"\"\"\n    on = np.zeros(NBINS, dtype=np.float32)\n    if len(starts) == 0:\n        return on\n    for a, b in zip(starts - go_time, stops - go_time):\n        if b <= BIN_EDGES[0] or a >= BIN_EDGES[-1]:\n            continue\n        # Overlap duration between [a, b] and every bin.  A plain \"does it touch the bin\"\n        # test would mark a bin that the interval overlaps by a fraction of a millisecond:\n        # photoinhibition ends at the go cue to within +-0.5 ms, which would otherwise\n        # switch the first post-go bin on for about half of the stimulated trials.\n        ov = np.minimum(b, BIN_EDGES[1:]) - np.maximum(a, BIN_EDGES[:-1])\n        on[ov > OVERLAP_TOL] = 1.0\n    return on\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 2 records this as a bug the sanity checks caught and fixed: photoinhibition\nends at the go cue to within ±0.5 ms and starts within ±0.5 ms of a bin edge, so the original\n\"does the interval touch this bin\" test switched the first *post*-go bin on for about half the\nstimulated trials and turned on one bin too early at the onset. Requiring > 1 ms of overlap\nremoves the artefact and makes the \"photostim always ends before the go cue\" check pass\nexactly. The AI also verified, and documented as not-a-bug, one trial whose laser onset is\n2.25 s pre-go because an early-lick replay pushed the go cue later while the laser fired at its\nusual time. The `--show-processing` panel 5 shows the stimulation confined to the delay epoch\n(−1.2 to −0.7 s) on 77/354 trials in the sample session.\n\n## 4-c. How is the `input` *Photostimulation* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The laser start/stop times are converted to go-cue-relative seconds (`starts - go_time`,\n`stops - go_time`) and compared against the same `BIN_EDGES` grid used to bin the spikes, for\nthe same curated `go` array. Only intervals overlapping the trial's own [−2.5, +1.5] s window\nare considered. So alignment is again structural, on one shared grid.\n\nii.\n```python\n            for j, g in enumerate(go):\n                m = (ps_stop > g + OFF_START) & (ps_start < g + OFF_END)\n                if m.any():\n                    photostim_on[j] = interval_overlap_bins(ps_start[m], ps_stop[m], g)\n```\n```python\n    for a, b in zip(starts - go_time, stops - go_time):\n        ...\n        ov = np.minimum(b, BIN_EDGES[1:]) - np.maximum(a, BIN_EDGES[:-1])\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 3(e): the reference also re-references `task_stimulation` to the go cue; the\nonly difference is that the reference keeps it as per-trial scalars while this conversion\nrasterises it onto the bin grid, \"because the decoder wants time-varying inputs\". Because the\ncomparison is against `BIN_EDGES` rather than `BIN_CENTERS`, the sub-millisecond tolerance\n(4-b) was needed to keep the rasterisation from leaking one bin past the go cue.\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction choice* derived from?\n\ni. A hit means the animal licked the instructed\nside, a miss means it licked the other side, and an `ignore` means it did not lick.\n\nii.\n```python\n        instruction = np.asarray(trials['trial_instruction'][:])\n        outcome = np.asarray(trials['outcome'][:])\n...\n        instr_k = instruction[keep_idx]\n        out_k = outcome[keep_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 4 (discrepancy table, \"`outcome` semantics\") documents that the AI validated this\nderivation against the raw lick-time streams before adopting it: on `hit` trials the animal\nlicks the instructed port (100%), on `miss` trials it *first* licks the opposite port (100%),\nand on `ignore` trials there are no licks in [go, go+1.5] (100%). Sanity check 13 re-ran the\nfirst-post-go-lick comparison on 5 spot-check sessions and got 100% agreement (195/195,\n353/353, 578/578, 573/573, …), and check 14 confirmed zero licks on \"no lick\" trials. So the\nderived variable is equivalent to the directly measured lick direction.\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction choice*?\n\ni. Coded 0 = left, 1 = right, 2 = no lick, with the default being `no lick` and hit/miss trials\noverwritten by the four instruction × outcome combinations. The per-trial value is then\nbroadcast across all 80 bins as row 0 of the per-trial output array (`int64`), and\n`output_values[0] = ['left', 'right', 'no lick']` names the codes. Resulting distribution:\nleft 0.429, right 0.422, no lick 0.149.\n\nii.\n```python\nCHOICE_LEFT, CHOICE_RIGHT, CHOICE_NOLICK = 0, 1, 2\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ['left', 'right', 'no lick'],\n    ...\n]\n```\n```python\n        # choice: hit -> instructed side, miss -> opposite side, ignore -> no lick\n        choice = np.full(n_trials, CHOICE_NOLICK, dtype=np.int64)\n        hit = out_k == 'hit'\n        miss = out_k == 'miss'\n        choice[hit & (instr_k == 'left')] = CHOICE_LEFT\n        choice[hit & (instr_k == 'right')] = CHOICE_RIGHT\n        choice[miss & (instr_k == 'left')] = CHOICE_RIGHT\n        choice[miss & (instr_k == 'right')] = CHOICE_LEFT\n```\n```python\n    outputs = [np.stack([np.full(NBINS, choice[j]),\n                         np.full(NBINS, outcome_code[j]),\n                         np.full(NBINS, early_code[j]),\n                         tongue_class[j]]).astype(np.int64)\n               for j in range(n_trials)]\n```\n\niii. The left/right/no-lick coding follows the instructions' ordering. The AI notes in\nStep 9 that the near-equal left/right split (0.429/0.422) is the expected signature of randomly\ninterleaved trial types, which it used as a consistency check.\n\n## 6-a.
